summary:
Seoul stands under South Korea's national framework. The country does not criminalise gender identity or gender expression in civilian life; consensual same-sex conduct between civilians is legal. The exception is the armed forces, where Military Criminal Act article 92-6 criminalises consensual same-sex conduct among military personnel with up to two years' imprisonment, a provision the Constitutional Court upheld in 2023. Enforcement has been punitive: in 2017 the military charged 32 personnel in what Amnesty International described as a gay witch hunt, and a gay soldier received a six-month prison sentence. Transgender people are excluded from military service altogether.

The sharpest documented harm to a trans person in the armed forces is the case of Staff Sergeant Byun Hui-su, compulsorily discharged in early 2020 after a military panel classified the effects of her gender-affirming surgery as a physical or mental handicap. She died by suicide in March 2021. The Daejeon District Court ruled the discharge unjust and reinstated her posthumously on 7 October 2021, and in March 2024 the Defence Ministry recognised her death as in the line of duty.

Restroom access is a live legal issue in Seoul. On 2 July 2024 the Seoul Central District Court, presiding judge Chung In-jae, dismissed the state's appeal and made final a ruling holding that police advice telling an LGBT person mid-legal-transition to avoid public restrooms for a while infringed personal rights. The court awarded the plaintiff 300,000 won of the 3 million won claimed, stating that the right to comfortably use restrooms is a fundamental and universal human right. The decision became final after neither party appealed.

The same problem appears in everyday practice. A 2021 National Human Rights Commission of Korea survey of 591 transgender respondents found that 41% used another-gender restrooms out of fear of mistreatment, 39% avoided food and drink to reduce the need, and 36% forwent restroom use altogether. A 2021 Pohang branch of the Daegu District Court ruling awarded 7 million won in damages against an academy that barred a trans student's restroom use.

Legal gender recognition is available and the surgical condition is falling away. On 8 May 2024 a court in Yeongdong approved male-to-female gender-marker changes for five transgender people without sex reassignment surgery, holding that it is against the law to determine gender change based on surgery and that every human being has the right to live according to their gender identity. The national court guidelines that previously required surgery have been downgraded to reference-only status, though some courts still apply them. The ruling sits outside Seoul and bears on Seoul as evidence of the national judicial trend. Earlier precedent had required persons seeking gender-affirming care to be over 20, single and without children, and on 24 November 2022 the Supreme Court ruled en banc that transgender individuals with minor children can have their gender legally recognised provided they are not married.

South Korean national law does not recognise same-sex marriage or civil unions, and same-sex couples cannot jointly adopt children. There is no comprehensive anti-discrimination law covering sexual orientation or gender identity. The government's position on care was tested in November 2023, when the National Human Rights Commission of Korea identified a transgender blind spot in hospitalisation after the Ministry of Health and Welfare rejected a request to draft hospitalisation guidelines for transgender patients, saying that accommodating diverse circumstances is difficult.

Violence concentrates at public events. In Incheon a Pride event ended in violence when about 1,000 Christian protestors attacked participants, and organisers later filed charges against pastors and accused police of inaction; at Busan's 2018 Pride some 2,000 police were deployed to protect 15,000 attendees from violent anti-gay protesters. In Seoul, the May 2020 Itaewon COVID-19 cluster saw contact tracing out LGBTQ people, after which doxing and online harassment rose; a trans-male bartender told NBC News he felt threatened walking on the street absent a nondiscrimination bill.

Discrimination burden is documented across life stages. A 2014 finding recorded that 54% of LGBTQ Korean youths were harassed by classmates, 16.1% of outed LGBTQ people were recommended conversion therapy, with 65.4% reporting harm and 94% psychological trauma, and a 2018 study found 51.5% of transgender adults faced harsh discrimination in the past year. Research from the youth LGBTQ+ centre DDing Dong, presented on 20 March 2024, shows trans teenagers avoid school restrooms for fear of being outed; a 16-year-old trans girl at a boys' school reported holding it in and leaving school early. A peer-reviewed nationwide survey published on 27 June 2025 in Epidemiology and Health, covering 585 transgender and non-binary young adults, documented a pervasive discrimination burden at school, work and in transition-related care. Human Rights Watch's World Report 2025 describes an overall relatively positive record on free media and civil society alongside persistent documented discrimination against LGBT people.
tangentialFactors:
The national pattern on restroom access runs in both directions within the judiciary: the Seoul Central District Court awarded 300,000 won against the state for police advice, while a Pohang branch of the Daegu District Court awarded 7 million won against a private academy for barring a trans student. Damages awards remain modest and symbolic rather than deterrent in scale.

Enforcement risk for trans visitors concentrates on documentation and outing rather than criminal law. Contact tracing during the May 2020 Itaewon cluster outed LGBTQ people and produced doxing and online harassment, an indication that public-health and police interactions can expose a person's status even where no offence exists.

Public events carry a demonstrated violence risk from organised anti-gay protest, with large police deployments recorded at Busan's 2018 Pride and allegations of police inaction at Incheon. Anti-discrimination legislation covering sexual orientation and gender identity remains absent at national level, which is the recurring gap cited by advocates and by a trans-male bartender quoted during the Itaewon outbreak.

Human Rights Watch's World Report 2025 places the country's record on free media and civil society as relatively positive alongside persistent documented discrimination against LGBT people, and LGBTI organisations can register, though an NGO won registration litigation at the Seoul Metropolitan Court in March 2017 and the government appealed onward, which Human Rights Watch described as years of bureaucratic obstruction.
localsOnly:
Residents face the military regime directly: transgender people are excluded from military service, and Military Criminal Act article 92-6 exposes serving personnel to up to two years' imprisonment for consensual same-sex conduct, upheld by the Constitutional Court in 2023. Staff Sergeant Byun Hui-su's compulsory discharge was ruled unjust and her post restored on 7 October 2021, and the Defence Ministry recognised her March 2021 death as in the line of duty in March 2024.

Gender-marker change no longer requires surgery as a matter of national court policy. The guidelines formerly demanding surgery were downgraded to reference-only status on the strength of rulings such as the 8 May 2024 Yeongdong decision for five plaintiffs, though some courts continue to apply them. The Supreme Court's en banc ruling of 24 November 2022 removed the bar on recognition for transgender parents of minor children provided they are unmarried, overturning an 11-year-old precedent.

Same-sex couples cannot marry or enter a civil union and cannot jointly adopt. A landmark 2024 Constitutional Court ruling on same-sex partners' healthcare rights is the main advance in that area.

Access to hospitalised care remains unsettled. In November 2023 the National Human Rights Commission of Korea identified a transgender blind spot after the Ministry of Health and Welfare declined to draft hospitalisation guidelines for transgender patients.

School environments are a documented site of harm. Trans teenagers avoid school restrooms for fear of being outed, and researchers from DDing Dong urged legal and institutional reform for safer school environments after presenting their findings on 20 March 2024. A nationwide survey of 585 transgender and non-binary young adults published on 27 June 2025 recorded discrimination across school, work and transition-related care.
outOfScopeNotes:
Whether the downgraded national court guidelines on surgery have in fact ceased to be applied in practice is unresolved: the source states only that some courts still apply them, without a count or a date.

The outcome of the NGO registration litigation after the March 2017 Seoul Metropolitan Court win and the government's onward appeal is not sourced here; the record shows the appeal was filed, not how it concluded.

No Seoul-specific figure for hate-crime charges, prosecutions or convictions arising from anti-LGBT violence at Pride events is available in this inventory. The Incheon organisers filed charges against pastors and accused police of inaction, but the disposition of those charges is not stated.

Visa, border-screening and entry-refusal practice for transgender visitors, including how gender markers on foreign passports are handled at Incheon and Gimpo airports, is not sourced and should be verified against current immigration guidance.
